sections.section: Phase 0: Scoping (which tool, what time-budget, what attendance)
rows: Select the right learning tool for the event
Operator names an event and asks "what kind of review" — apply the four-tool ladder (AAR / RLS / FLA / Learning Review), scaled by learning opportunity not outcome severity.
Choose informal AAR for small in-team learning
A platoon-level-and-below event; an on-the-spot informal AAR uses the same format as a formal one with minimal resources and gives immediate feedback while the training is fresh.
Choose formal AAR for high-stakes cross-functional incident
Formal-AAR 6-8 week lead time; two-levels-above rule for external evaluations; experience-over-rank OC selection.
Convene without administrative-action contamination
The guide requires an explicit no-punitive-action commitment in the signed delegation of authority and calls the firewall critical: information is the lifeblood of safety.
Hold the default-to-system posture before the conversation begins
"Action singling out an individual is rarely appropriate — most patient safety issues have deeper causes and require wider action." Read this aloud before scoping.
Budget time honestly for the depth required
The TC's planning allowances: 30-45 min platoon, 1 hr company, 2 hr battalion-and-above. Match duration to depth.
Set the climate and spirit as operational concern
Climate of an AAR is load-bearing, not soft skill; the AAR is professional discussion, not critique.
Identify the fratricide-equivalent topics
What events in your domain must always be discussed in detail, in a review held as soon as possible after they happen? Name them in advance, not after the fact.
Establish the Ten Principles and Agreements
Group-dialogue agreements as the precondition for honest accounts; explain the FLA process and discuss all ten before the dialogue opens.
Scope as cross-functional rather than team-internal

Scrum's Sprint Retrospective inspects the team's own way of working, sprint by sprint; the AAR is its event-triggered, cross-functional counterpart, so team-internal iterative learning routes to [[retro]] instead.
Surface the senior's stance on mistakes before accounts begin

Operator asks how to convene without administrative-action contamination: MCDP 1 ties candour to the senior's tolerance ("a subordinate's willingness to admit mistakes depends on the commander's willingness to tolerate them"); pair with LFUO's no-punitive-action assurance for the procedure.
Hold the review while memory is fresh, successes included
Operator describes time pressure tempting them to skip: MCDP 1 holds critiques "immediately after completing training, before memory of the events has faded", after success as well as failure.
Choose the discussion-organisation technique for this event
Three options — chronological for narrative recall, BOS-equivalent for systemic patterns across phases, key events for tight-focus when time is limited.
Decompose pre-event beliefs, perceptions, expectations, paradigms
Surface the participants' pre-event situational awareness; four-category decomposition makes invisible mental models visible.
Build the timeline through the Five Hows

Structured decision-reconstruction tool inside the Lessons Learned Analysis: for each key decision, explore how and why choices that seemed wrong in hindsight "were actually valid or at least legitimate in context at the time"; consensus is not the goal.
Treat divergent accounts as evidence, not problem
The AAR is multi-perspective discovery; "no commander, no matter how skilled, will see as much as the individual soldiers and leaders who actually conduct the training."
Apply the deflection-question protocol for emotional recall

Do not take the interview deeper into traumatic recall (the guide leaves that to mental health professionals); if the participant goes there anyway, deflect to something that went right or that they know well, and make sure they know how to reach mental health support.
Interview before hindsight contaminates accounts
Interview as soon as possible; Roese & Vohs 2012 borrowed-through citation on hindsight bias.
Surface attribution and perception biases in participant accounts
Reach for the OB framing on perception (perceptual selectivity, functional background), fundamental attribution error, self-serving bias.
Use open-ended questions, not yes/no
Question-design contrast: *"What happened when X?"* (invites narrative) over *"Why didn't you Y?"* (invites self-defence).
Surface mental-model diversity in the room
Each participant holds a partial-but-valid model; surface each vantage point separately *before* integrating the accounts.
Build a shared model of the system the team can hold

When accounts compete and the group needs a shared picture — Rich Pictures first for low-overhead collective externalisation, then a CLD once the group is ready to negotiate causal links; the map is a boundary object the group argues with instead of with each other.
Distinguish facilitative from transmissive question framing
Ch 1's shift from direct to facilitative teaching, applied to AAR questions: does the question carry the facilitator's conclusion, or open the participant's account?
Recognise hindsight bias contaminating the analysis
Hindsight bias, availability heuristic, anchoring — the perception and memory frame for facilitator vocabulary.
Put the reasons and the intent on the timeline

Operator describes building a timeline: for each action, record what the person was trying to achieve and why the move made sense; MCDP 1's critique focuses "not so much on the actions we took as on why we took those actions and why they brought the results they did".
Weigh accounts by where each person stood

Operator describes participant accounts diverging: all hands contribute; a competent person at the point of decision better appreciates the true situation than a senior some distance away; everyone acted on incomplete, inaccurate or contradictory information.
Refuse the "root cause" framing
"Cause isn't something investigators 'find' or 'discover'; cause is always something we create by recreating the event"; *networked causality* as the replacement vocabulary.
Refuse counterfactual reasoning
"If this person had done X, then the outcome would have been Y and the accident would not have occurred" is the forbidden move; learn why people did what they actually did.
Apply contributory-factors-not-the-cause framing

TC 25-20 takes no position on single versus multiple causes; its discussion techniques (chronological, BOS across phases) let several contributing actions surface. Ask what else contributed besides the first explanation offered.
Look for multiple improbable events
"Most often, the Lessons Learned Analysis will reveal that multiple improbable events were necessary for the accident to occur." Resist single-cause anchoring.
Test the situation against system archetypes
Five named patterns — Fixes that Fail, Success to the Successful, Shifting the Burden, Drifting Goals, Limits to Growth. Use as hypothesis-generators, not labels.
Map the feedback loops producing the pattern

Replace the X-causes-Y frame with a structural read: what feedback structure kept the problem in place, and which loop would bring it back if the named cause were fixed? The CLD is a hypothesis to revise.
Generate a CLD or other systems-map artefact for contributory factors
When the contributory factors form feedback loops (a CLD is less useful where loops are absent or unimportant); PSM submap analysis focuses a large map on particular questions or issues.
Surface accumulated history shaping the current state
Ignoring accumulated history is the failure mode: the incident surfaced from accumulated stocks (trust, fatigue, degraded margin), not from nowhere.
Apply Five Whys with surprise-as-progress-signal
At an AAR, check 5-Whys depth by surprise: "If you're rarely surprised by your root causes, you may not be digging deep enough."
Separate the individual's action from the conditions the tree tests
Contributors sit either in the individual's action or in the conditions the tree tests (protocols under Q3; peer behaviour, training and supervision under Q4); both belong in the analysis.
Read software-incident contributory factors against empirical patterns
Reliability statistics — bi-exponential fault-report duplicates pattern; survival-adjusted maintenance-to-development ratio; cone of uncertainty as artefact.
Locate decision-rights ambiguity as contributory factor
RACI matrix built for the moment of failure: did anyone hold the Responsible and Accountable cells for the step that failed, or were they empty or contested?
Identify code-smell-shaped design-debt contributors
Eleven named code smells with refactoring prescriptions; the smell vocabulary lets the team name what kept compounding.
Detect Goodhart's-Law-shaped contributory factor
A metric was being treated as a target and collapsed under control pressure; the measurement itself contributed.
Hold the whole system in view (Deming + Goldratt borrowed-through)
"No single part of a system can ever bring overall improvement"; Holistic / Systemic value gives the substrate for system-level contributory factors.
Name an org-structure contributory factor with archetype precision

The LLA has surfaced that a team-archetype mismatch (e.g. CAPS-2 team asked to deliver CAPS-3 outcomes) was among the multiple improbable events; OT gives the naming vocabulary that "the team was siloed" and "communication broke down" lack.
Identify topology-mismatch as a recurring contributory-factor pattern
The incident shows a pattern of Resource-Topology drag (utilisation-optimised structure asked for discovery or speed) or Delivery-Topology absent-outcome-validation.
Name the local-optimisation amplifier among contributory factors

Multiple individually-defensible org-design choices (a reward structure, a policy, a reporting line) combined to produce the incident; OT's local-optimisation warning names the pattern ("performance of the whole system may actually decline").
Identify single-team-island structure as a contributory factor source

A previously-fixed team keeps failing inside an unchanged surrounding system; the Primer's warning applies — fixing the team alone leaves the surround's structures, processes and contributory factors untouched.
Test whether Resource-Topology framing of frontline staff contributed

Frontline staff were being treated as fungible resources (rotated, denied voice in design, denied end-to-end accountability); the Resource-framing is a named structural contributory factor, not a leadership-style critique.
Widen a single cause to many forces and self-made friction

Operator describes a single-cause analysis: MCDP 1 treats each episode as "the unique product of myriad moral, mental, and physical forces"; prompt for self-induced friction (unclear goal, poor coordination, unclear or complicated plans, complex task organisation or command relationships, complicated technology).
Show that waiting carried risk too

Operator describes counterfactual creeping in: where the counterfactual assumes waiting was safe, MCDP 1's "Risk is equally common to action and inaction" answers it; LFUO carries the rule against counterfactuals itself.
Walk the five-test decision tree in order
An individual action concern is on the table; Q1 (deliberate harm) → Q2 (health) → Q3 (foresight) → Q4 (substitution) → Q5 (mitigation) applied sequentially.
Apply the foresight test as system-contract probe
Is there a protocol; is it workable and in routine use; did the individual knowingly depart? All three Yes to advance to substitution test.
Apply the substitution test as peer-and-supervision probe

Would peers in same circumstances have behaved similarly; was training missed; was supervision absent? Any Yes routes to Recommendation E: singling out the individual is unlikely to be appropriate, and wider actions may include, but not be limited to, the individual.
Decompose a multi-action incident into one-action evaluations
Multiple actions or omissions bound up in a single incident; each must be evaluated through the tree separately, not jointly.
Test the reckless-and-willful threshold

The FLA termination threshold (conduct that is intentional, unjustifiable, and done with foreknowledge that it was likely to result in serious harm, death or injury); the guide expects it to be highly unlikely; below it FLA continues, at/above it terminates.
Terminate the learning analysis on culpability grounds
If the reckless-and-willful threshold is met, the FLA terminates and interview notes go to the lead facilitator for confidential and secure storage.
Select the recommendation end-state from the just-culture tree
Seven end-states (A deliberate-harm through G residual management action); the choice names the response, paired with parallel wider-investigation obligation.
Communicate the just-culture decision to stakeholders

The guide is both decision aid and communication tool, shared with all parties in advance; its dual purpose is protecting staff from unfair targeting and protecting patients by not treating wider patient safety issues as individual issues.
Name which kind of error is on the table

Operator surfaces an individual-vs-system call: MCDP 1 separates overbold errors (dealt with leniently), errors of inaction or timidity (dealt with severely) and stupid or reckless acts (no licence); use it to bring waits into scope, and route the individual-action decision to the NHS tree.
Read the just-culture call against organisational behaviour substrate

The fundamental attribution error pushes observers toward blaming the individual rather than the situation, and self-serving bias leads each function to attribute the failure to adjacent teams; surface both before deciding.
Frame actions through Blameless Postmortem
"Our job is not to point fingers"; two foundations — information availability + psychological safety.
Hold the FLA / Learning Review boundary on recommendations
Recommendations require Learning Review with focus groups, optional academic SMEs, Learning Review Board, Safety Action Plan; an FLA cannot produce them.
Treat critical capabilities as stop-rules, not gradients
Critical gate tasks (CATS): performance below standard is a stop, not a partial score. Identify gate-task equivalents and honour the stop.
Allocate retraining resources to weakness, not strength
Put training priority on new or deficient tasks; the TC still names sustaining proficiency on tasks already at standard as important, just less so.
Surface ownership ambiguity before adjourning
LS Discovery & Action Dialogues' closing question: *"Who will do what when next?"* — refuses adjournment without named owner.
Resolve decision-rights ambiguity in action ownership
RACI matrix (Responsible / Accountable / Consulted / Informed) for ambiguous-ownership actions.
Surface latent dissent before commit
Fist of five six-level voting before commit — *two or fewer fingers is the cue to stop, discuss and re-vote*; surfaces latent dissent the meeting tone is suppressing.
Frame escalation to leadership when contributors are above team authority
The six structure types + organisational-design primitives; name the right interlocutor for the structural change being requested.
Frame the action's stakeholder-prioritisation
Grunig-Hunt categories with power × interest and exigency prioritisation (Ch 3.2, Ch 3.3) when actions cross multiple stakeholder interests; Donaldson-Preston three approaches.
Frame ethical exposure surfaced by the AAR
When the AAR has surfaced safety-obligation, whistleblower-protection, or known-but-unreported-problem questions, the ethical substrate names them.
Avoid AI overconfidence in proposed actions

When an AI system contributed: Evals (against AI overconfidence) and Human-in-the-Loop (against silent AI delegation) name what the actions must address, the confidence the AI's outputs carried and where the human review gates sat; Design of Experiments makes each action a testable experiment.
Frame the action through Establish Shared Principles
Against copy-without-principles: the action is grounded in the underlying principle, not just the surface practice.
Limit the number of actions
Reduce the Batch Size practice: focus and limit the number of things in progress; commit to few actions and finish them.
Decide improvement-investment allocation for software-incident root themes
Survival-adjusted break-even applied to code or architecture improvements meant to cut future maintenance cost; the survival rate of the system shapes the investment horizon.
Frame structural-remediation actions as Elevating-Kata experiments

Structural actions are framed as "thoughtful experiments" with named hypotheses and checkpoints, not pronouncements; pairs with LFUO Learning-Review-required-for-recommendations constraint for structural changes.
Frame escalation of org-design contributory factors to leadership

Escalation memo frames the ask as "the leaders who own the business objective also own the structural fix" — converts a structural FYI into a leadership action item; pairs with OpenStax PoM for structure catalogue.
Use named-archetype vocabulary in escalation memos to non-engineering leadership

Precise archetype labels (CAPS-2 → CAPS-3) survive transit to leadership not engaged in the incident; avoids vague language ("more autonomy", "cross-functional teams") that gets escalation memos dismissed.
Defend against single-element structural fixes in action design

A proposed remediation that changes only one org-design element (a role, a policy, a committee) without systems-fit carries the local-optimisation warning: "flow can get worse." The action needs to address systems-fit.
Test actions for added control and equipment-only fixes

Operator describes drafting actions: "Better equipment is not the cure for all ills"; information technology tempts toward precise, positive control; people oversupervised in routine work cannot be expected to show initiative in the field.
Close with What/So What/Now What sequenced debrief

Three-question sequence (included in many Center for Creative Leadership programs, borrowed-through; explicitly named *After Action Debrief* in the handbook); refuses jumping to Now-What before What and So-What.
Apply TC 25-20 closing-comments rule
Leader summarises key points, ends positively, links to next training, then leaves so the unit can discuss in private.
Lock in the next-action commitment before the review ends
The real benefits live in follow-up; an AAR without a clear retraining commitment leaves them unrealised.
Mark delayed retraining as visible and timed
If retraining is deferred, the people involved must understand the task was not performed to standard and that retraining will occur; keep the deferral timed and communicated, not silent.
Revise SOPs surfaced by the review
If the AAR has surfaced SOP problems, the SOP must be revised and the change implemented during the next iteration.
Keep room for judgement in a revised SOP

Operator describes the AAR surfacing SOP problems: MCDP 1 lists standing operating procedures as one means of fighting despite uncertainty, alongside simple, flexible plans, contingency planning and fostering initiative; write the purpose into the revised step.
Open the response zone for the helpless team

15% Solutions reframes locus-of-control: *"Where do you have freedom to act? What's in your 15%?"* (the handbook's own question; it separately quotes Gareth Morgan on "15-percent initiatives", borrowed-through).
Confirm learning as precondition for continuous improvement

"Learning is the key concept before continuous improvement can ever happen!"; the source offers Retrospectives, Strategy Meetings or Kaizen Groups as optional forms and the AAR is one such form; an action list without shared learning has not produced its benefit.
Frame the AAR as discovery, not critique
A critique transmits one viewpoint and stifles learning; the AAR aggregates and tests views across all participants, who discover for themselves what happened.
Address force protection (safety) at every AAR
Standing-agenda discipline: safety touched every review regardless of whether it came up during the event under review.
Schedule OT re-mapping to test whether structural recommendations took hold

"Periodic re-mapping with Org Topologies is an easy and fast way to complete a learning loop of feedback and adapting" — did the topology actually shift, or did the structural change stall at announcement? Tie re-mapping to a calendar date and a participant list.
Cross-link to the iterative team-internal cadence
When the team also needs iterative team-internal learning at retrospective cadence, route to the retro axis.
